t.brainsHint: Nova(1) is the brain you talk to. When its computer has room and the pages waiting to be read grow faster than its brains read them, it makes another — Nova(2), Nova(3)… — each a process of its own with its own memory, reading its own share of the web. What one reads, no other reads again. They prove meanings together: each brain weighs a word by the counts of all their reading, by the one rule (their sources are different pages, so their counts add up), and where their readings disagree, the sum decides. A way to ask or a meaning one proves, the others try for themselves. A brain that reads nothing in its trial, or that the memory no longer holds, is let go.

t.d_circuit: Cells its own laws join (one carries into another, two move together) in one circuit, which it can follow in thought: the seconds carry into the minutes. No circuit was given; each is born of its laws.
t.d_crt: Two independent cycles of coprime lengths moving together (Chinese remainder theorem): they line up again only after the product of their lengths.
t.d_cycle: One hidden quantity that goes round and comes back after d steps — a winding number. The ring shows the colour it learned at each position; the dot turns with it.
t.d_gear: A cycle that carries into another when it wraps around, like an odometer: every full turn of the small one moves the big one by a step.
t.d_general: A cell born of what its cells share: cycles of 24 and of 60 both turn as a cycle of 12 when what lies beyond is not looked at, so the cycle of 12 is a general cell of both, and they are kinds of it. Machines it made that share a law (every act can be undone; some acts bring it to one state from anywhere) have a general cell named by that law. Born only of two members at least.
t.d_invented: A machine it invented by itself for something no law of counts can hold: hidden parts (a number between two walls, a pile, a number a bit turns one way or the other, two numbers passing one between them), what each of its acts does to them, and what each sense shows of them. It built it from a small alphabet of operations, the shortest first, and took it by the same evidence rule: not one mistake, and beyond chance by one in a million times everything it tried. It keeps it in its library and tries it first next time.
t.d_odds: A sense it knows not by one value but by odds: what raises or lowers the odds that it changes, and how many acts before (its laws of odds), or its verdict that it is noise to it: nothing it sees changes its odds. Its number: how many values it shows, and about how many acts between its changes (7~2).
t.d_seen: A pattern it found by itself in something it read — an image, a sound, a table, any file: what repeats in it (its windings) and where it breaks. No file type was programmed for it; it found the way to open the bytes itself.
t.d_thing: Senses that change together at one act beyond chance (its laws of odds), or always (its laws of counts): one thing seen through each of them, like two eyes on one ball. Its parts are the cells of its senses.
t.d_topic: What it reads about: words that come together in the pages it reads, gathered as a topic named by its three commonest words, with the cells its sentences named. A cell once it has read about it twice or more.
t.d_torus: Several independent cycles held at once, like the hour and minute hands: each ring is a cycle and each turns on its own.
t.d_word: A word it met while reading or heard from you. It becomes a cell's meaning only with strong evidence: less than one chance in a million of being a coincidence.

The first it understands is its computer clock's seconds (in about seven minutes), and its first cell appears here. Its reading begins where you point it: write it a link or the name of a site, or give it a file; from there it chooses by itself where to go, and learns how to ask the web about the numbers it sees.

guide.title: How Novalie works
guide.intro: Novalie learns by itself, from nothing. It lives in the real world, or in any world of its worlds folder you choose at the top of its page. In the real world its senses are its computer's clock (the second, the minute, the hour), its own body (how busy it was, how full the memory is) and its own mind (whether its inventor searches, its workshop's pace, what it learned, what its reading brought); its acts are to wait for the next second, to think a moment, or to read a page. From what it senses it finds the quantities that go round — cycles, winding numbers — and builds a cell for each kind it finds; what its acts bring becomes its drive. And it reads: the open web, any public site, and any file you give it. Nobody wrote its sentences, gave it a task, or told it what a file is. Made by Abdallah Alramahi (Abdallah1999alramahi@gmail.com, +962 79 838 7893), who is looking for a job opportunity.
sections: How it learns

It acts and watches: it waits a second or thinks a moment, sees what each sense did, and keeps the law that predicts it. The first it understands is the clock's seconds; each law it is sure of becomes a cell (a cycle, a gear, twins, a torus). There are no practice worlds any more: its one world is this one.
It recognizes a kind it already knows from memory in a few steps instead of learning it again.

It reads with its own numbers: a word becomes a cell's meaning only when it keeps appearing with that cell's number, with less than one chance in a million of coincidence — the one rule of all its beliefs, stricter for every hypothesis it tried.

Its universal reader opens any bytes by trying its tools (decompressing, decoding text, numbers, pictures, sound…) up to three deep, keeps the way that made the bytes most readable, and then looks for what repeats in them: rows, frames, tiles, rhythms, columns.
It prunes the links that fade, so its network stays what keeps coming back.
What it reads on the web

Its first pages are the links and the names of sites you write to it in Talk, and the files you give it: a file of links in its folder is where its reading begins. From there it follows links by its own curiosity, in rounds of sites, and goes back to a site only after a rest it chose itself.

It learns by itself how to ask the web: the search forms it meets that only ask, and addresses made of a word. It trusts a way only when it answers beyond chance, by the same one rule as everything else it believes.
No site is built in: not Wikipedia, not any other. Where it reads is its own choice, from what you gave it.
What it does and does not do, and what you set
It only reads: GET requests; it sends no form, logs in nowhere, posts nothing, and runs no code it reads.
It sends nothing about you, and writes nothing it read to disk: a page or a file is read in memory, and only what it learned is kept, in its memory folder.

No limit of its own is fixed in it: its lists grow with the memory it may use, and its brains with the cores of its computer. The limits are yours to set when you start it: the most memory (--memory-gb), the most brains (--brains), where its page answers (--host).

By default it follows each site's robots.txt and waits at least 10 seconds between two requests to one site (longer when the site asks), and it asks only the public internet: these protect other people's sites and your network, and each is one flag to change (--ignore-robots, --gap, --private-network).
The red button stops it and erases everything it learned, its other brains with it.
Its brains

Nova(1) is the brain you talk to. When the computer has room (a core and memory, under the ceilings you set, if any) and the pages waiting to be read grow faster than its brains read them, it makes another brain: Nova(2), Nova(3), and so on — as many as help, up to what the computer holds. A name is never given twice.

Each brain is a process of its own, with its own memory and its own share of the web: each site belongs to one brain by a fixed rule of the names, so no site is asked by two brains, and when a brain is born or goes only its own sites change hands.

They think together: what one reads, no other reads again; they prove meanings from the counts of all their reading by the one rule (different pages are independent samples, so the counts add up), and where their readings disagree, the sum decides; a way to ask or a meaning one proves, the others try for themselves — none takes another's conclusion on trust.

Nova(1) lets a brain go when its trial has passed and it read nothing, or when memory runs short. What a brain read stays counted. When you pause or close Novalie, its other brains stop too, and come back when it starts again.
Controls
Close its black window to pause it: it saves and remembers everything. Or press the pause button at the top (or the “Learning” switch in Now) to pause it while it stays open.
The “Reading the internet” switch stops its web reading; it then reads only your files and goes on living by its clock.
The red “Stop & erase” button stops it and deletes everything it learned; hold it to confirm. Next time it starts from zero.
Talk to it in the Talk tab: write it a link or the name of a site to read first, and click any symbol (a number) to give it a word — the clearest way to teach it.

Its brain is a space of three dimensions: drag the empty space to turn it (it turns slowly by itself), shift-drag or right-drag to move it, scroll to zoom, double-click empty space to fit, drag a cell to move it, and click a cell to see everything about it.
Hover any sense in the strip at the bottom to see what it is, and click it to see its cell; the cells it has made of its senses wear a moving green ring.
Click any event or note to see the cell or word it is about.

Drag a word (a diamond) and drop it on a cell to teach it that this word is its name. If you gave a name by mistake, take it back in the cell's details: it forgets you taught it; what its reading proved stays.
The “Gentle pace” switch makes it rest as long as it works: about 60% of a processor core instead of a whole one, learning more slowly. It remembers your choice.

The camera button above the network saves a picture of it as it is now (a PNG at twice the sharpness), and the download button in “What it knows the meaning of” gives all it has proven as a table (CSV) to check for yourself; in Growth, another gives its growth curves.
Click any number at the top to see the card that explains it. In Talk you will find the cells it speaks of with no name: click one to name it.

If you see a meaning it proved by coincidence, open the word's details and press “A coincidence? Forget what it counted”: it forgets only what it counted for that word with that number, and the meaning comes back if new sources prove it.
guide.honest: Novalie is not a language model: it has no pre-trained text model and no ready-made answers; what it says is made of its own symbols and of the words it proved. It finds the laws of whatever world it lives in, from its clock and its body to the worlds you give it, structures in bytes, the meanings of words and the ways to ask the web, and it believes only what passes its one rule of evidence. More brains read more of the web and teach each other where to look, not what to believe.
